source_text: Ἄλλο γὰρ τὸ ἐν ἀμπέλῳ γλυκὺ, καὶ ἄλλο τὸ ἐν μηλέᾳ, καὶ σύκῳ, καὶ φοίνικι. Ἔτι σε βούλομαι περὶ τὴν ἐξέτασιν ταύτην φιλοτεχνῆσαι, πῶς τὸ αὐτὸ ὕδωρ νῦν μὲν λεῖόν ἐστι τῇ αἰσθήσει, ὅταν ἐν τοῖσδέ τισι τοῖς φυτοῖς γενόμενον ἀπογλυκανθῇ· νῦν δὲ πληκτικόν ἐστι τῆς γεύσεως, ὅταν δι' ἄλλων φυτῶν ἐνεχθὲν ἀποξύνηται. Καὶ πάλιν εἰς τὴν ἐσχάτην πικρότητα μεταβάλλον ἐκτραχύνει τὴν αἴσθησιν, ὅταν ἐν ἀψίνθῳ ἢ σκαμμωνίᾳ γένηται. Καὶ ἐν μὲν ταῖς βαλάνοις, ἢ τῷ καρπῷ τῆς κρανείας, πρὸς τὴν στυφὴν καὶ αὐστηρὰν ποιότητα μεταβάλλει· ἐν δὲ ταῖς τερεβίνθοις, καὶ ταῖς καρύαις, πρὸς ἁπαλὴν καὶ ἐλαιώδη φύσιν μεθίσταται. 5.9 Καὶ τί δεῖ τὰ πόρρω λέγειν, ὅπου γε ἐπὶ τῆς αὐτῆς συκῆς πρὸς τὰς ἐναντιωτάτας μεταβαίνει ποιότητας; Πικρότατον μὲν γάρ ἐστιν ἐν τῷ ὀπῷ, γλυκύτατον δὲ ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ καρπῷ. Καὶ ἐπὶ τῆς ἀμπέλου στυπτικώτατον μὲν ἐπὶ τῶν ἀκρεμόνων, ἥδιστον δὲ ἐν τοῖς βότρυσιν. Αἱ δὲ κατὰ τὰς χρόας διαφοραὶ, πόσαι; Ἴδοις ἂν ἐν λειμῶνι τὸ αὐτὸ ὕδωρ ἐρυθραινόμενον μὲν ἐν τῷδε τῷ ἄνθει, καὶ ἐν ἄλλῳ πορφυροῦν, καὶ κυανὸν ἐν τῷδε, καὶ ἐν ἑτέρῳ λευκόν· καὶ πλείονα πάλιν τῆς ἐν ταῖς χρόαις ποικιλίας, τὴν κατὰ τὰς ὀδμὰς διαφορὰν παρεχόμενον. Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ὁρῶ μοι τὸν λόγον τῇ ἀπληστίᾳ τῆς θεωρίας εἰς ἀμετρίαν ἐκπίπτοντα, ὃν ἐὰν μὴ δήσας πρὸς ἀνάγκην ἀπαγάγω τῆς κτίσεως, ἐπιλείψει με ἡ ἡμέρα τὴν μεγάλην σοφίαν ἐκ τῶν μικρο τάτων ὑμῖν παριστῶντα. Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ ξύλον κάρπιμον, ποιοῦν καρπὸν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς. Καὶ εὐθὺς αἱ κορυφαὶ τῶν ὀρέων ἐκόμων· καὶ ἐφιλοτεχνοῦντο παράδεισοι, καὶ ποταμῶν ὄχθαι μυρίοις γένεσι φυτῶν ὡραΐζοντο. Καὶ τὰ μὲν τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην ηὐτρέπιστο κατακοσμῆσαι τράπεζαν· τὰ δὲ βοσκήμασι τροφὴν παρεσκεύαζεν, ἐκ τῶν φύλλων, ἐκ τῶν καρπῶν. Ἄλλα τὰς ἐκ τῆς ἰατρικῆς ὠφελείας ἡμῖν προεξένει· τοὺς χυλοὺς, τοὺς ὀποὺς, τὰ κάρφη, τοὺς φλοιοὺς, τὸν καρπόν· καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ὅσα ἡμῖν ἡ χρονία πεῖρα ἐξεῦρεν, ἐκ τῶν κατὰ μέρος περιπτώσεων συλλεγομένη τὸ χρήσιμον, ταῦτα ἡ ὀξεῖα τοῦ κτίσαντος πρόνοια, ἐξ ἀρχῆς προβλεψαμένη, εἰς γένεσιν ἤγαγε. Σὺ δὲ ὅταν ἴδῃς τὰ ἥμερα, τὰ ἄγρια, τὰ φίλυδρα, τὰ χερσαῖα, τὰ ἀνθοφοροῦντα, ἢ τὰ ἀνάνθη, ἐν μικρῷ τὸν μέγαν ἐπιγινώσκων, πρόσθες ἀεὶ τῷ θαύματι, καὶ αὔξησόν μοι τὴν ἀγάπην τοῦ κτίσαντος. Ἐξέταζε πῶς τὰ μὲν ἀειθαλῆ ἐποίησε, τὰ δὲ γυμνούμενα· καὶ τῶν ἀειθαλῶν τὰ μὲν φυλλοβόλα, τὰ δὲ ἀείφυλλα. Φυλλοβολεῖ γὰρ καὶ ἐλαία καὶ πίτυς, εἰ καὶ λεληθότως ὑπαλλάσσει τὰ φύλλα, ὥστε μηδέποτε δοκεῖν τῆς κομῆς ἀπογυμνοῦσθαι. Ἀείφυλλον δὲ ὁ φοίνιξ, τῷ αὐτῷ φύλλῳ ἐκ τῆς πρώτης βλαστήσεως εἰς τέλος συμπαραμένων. Ἔπειτα κἀκεῖνο σκόπει, πῶς ἡ μυρίκη ὥσπερ ἀμφίβιόν ἐστι, καὶ τοῖς φιλύδροις συναριθμούμενον, καὶ κατὰ τὰς ἐρήμους πληθυνόμενον. Διὸ καὶ ὁ Ἱερεμίας διαίως τὰ πονηρότερα καὶ ἐπαμφοτερίζοντα τῶν ἠθῶν τῷ τοιούτῳ φυτῷ παρεικάζει. 5.10 Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ. Τὸ μικρὸν τοῦτο πρόσταγμα εὐθὺς φύσις μεγάλη καὶ λόγος ἔντεχνος ἦν, θᾶττον τοῦ ἡμετέρου νοήματος τὰς μυρίας τῶν φυομένων ἰδιότητας ἐκτελῶν.
thought_title: One water, many tastes and colors in plants
orientation: Basil is expounding the third day of creation, showing how the same water produces different qualities in different plants, and then turns to the command 'Let the earth bring forth' as the source of all plant life.
pass_a_gloss: For one thing is the sweet in the vine, and another the sweet in the apple tree, and in the fig, and in the palm. Still I want you to be industrious about this examination, how the same water is now smooth to the sense, when it has become sweetened after coming to be in these certain plants; but now it is striking to the taste, when it is made sour after being carried through other plants. And again changing into the utmost bitterness it roughens the sense, when it comes to be in wormwood or scammony. And in acorns, or the fruit of the cornel tree, it changes toward the astringent and harsh quality; but in terebinths and walnut trees, it is transformed toward a soft and oily nature. And why is it necessary to speak of things far off, when indeed on the same fig tree it passes over to the most opposite qualities? For it is most bitter in the sap, but sweetest in the fruit itself. And on the vine it is most astringent on the shoots, but sweetest in the grape clusters. And the differences according to colors, how many are they? You might see in a meadow the same water being made red in this flower, and in another purple, and dark blue in this one, and in another white; and again providing a greater difference according to smells than the variety in colors. But indeed I see my discourse falling into excess by the insatiability of contemplation, which unless I bind it and lead it back to the necessity of the creation, the day will fail me as I present to you the great wisdom from the smallest things. Let the earth bring forth a fruit-bearing tree, making fruit upon the earth. And immediately the peaks of the mountains were covered with foliage; and gardens were being artfully made, and riverbanks were being adorned with countless kinds of plants. And some things had been prepared to adorn the human table; but other things were providing food for cattle, from the leaves, from the fruits. Other things were furnishing to us the benefits from medicine: the juices, the saps, the twigs, the barks, the fruit; and simply all things that long experience discovered for us, gathering the useful from particular occurrences, these things the sharp forethought of the Creator, having foreseen from the beginning, brought into being. But you, whenever you see the tame plants, the wild plants, the water-loving plants, the dry-land plants, the flowering plants, or the flowerless plants, recognizing the great one in the small, always add to the wonder, and increase for me the love of the Creator. Examine how he made some evergreen, but others being stripped bare; and of the evergreen, some shedding leaves, but others ever-leafed. For both the olive and the pine shed leaves, even if they exchange the leaves imperceptibly, so that they never seem to be stripped of their foliage. But the palm is ever-leafed, remaining with the same leaf from the first sprouting to the end. Then consider also that, how the tamarisk is like an amphibious thing, both being numbered among the water-loving plants, and multiplying in the deserts. Therefore also Jeremiah fittingly compares the more wicked and wavering characters to such a plant. Let the earth bring forth. This small command was immediately a great nature and an artful principle, completing the countless peculiarities of the things that grow more quickly than our thought.

choices.why: Keeps the substantivized adjective as a quality residing in each plant, matching Basil's point that the same water takes on different qualities in different plants.
rejected: what is sweet in the vine

choices.english: it is striking to the taste
choices.why: Preserves the active, aggressive force of πληκτικός (striking, sharp) rather than softening it to a mere taste descriptor.
rejected: it is sharp to the taste

choices.why: Keeps the physical metaphor of roughness applied to sensation, which Basil uses to describe extreme bitterness.
Renders ἀπληστία literally as insatiability, preserving Basil's self-critical image of being carried away by the delight of examining nature.
rejected: by the boundless appetite for speculation

choices.english: a great nature and an artful principle
choices.why: Keeps both nouns distinct: φύσις as the created nature that results, and λόγος as the rational, artful principle embedded in the command.
rejected: a great natural force and a skillful design
a mighty nature and a cunning word

choices.why: Renders ἐπαμφοτερίζοντα as wavering between two sides, matching the tamarisk's amphibious quality that Basil applies to moral character.

bible_refs.note: Βλαστησάτω ἡ γῆ ξύλον κάρπιμον, ποιοῦν καρπὸν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
Basil refers to Jeremiah comparing wicked and wavering characters to the tamarisk (μυρίκη)

pass_b_english: For the sweet quality in the vine is one thing, and that in the apple tree, the fig, and the date palm is another. I want you to linger with me over this inquiry a little longer: how the same water is smooth to the senses at one moment, when it becomes sweetened in certain plants, and at another moment it is striking to the taste, when it is made sour as it passes through other plants. And again, when it changes into extreme bitterness, it roughens the sense, as happens in wormwood or scammony. In acorns, or the fruit of the cornel tree, it changes into an astringent and harsh quality; but in terebinths and walnut trees, it is transformed into a soft and oily nature.

And why speak of distant examples, when in the same fig tree it passes over into the most opposite qualities? For it is most bitter in the sap, but most sweet in the fruit itself. And on the vine it is most astringent in the shoots, but most pleasant in the grape clusters. And how many are the differences in colors? You could see in a meadow the same water reddened in one flower, and in another purple, and dark blue in this one, and white in another; and again it provides a difference in scents that is even greater than the variety in colors.

But I see that my discourse is falling into excess through the insatiability of contemplation. Unless I bind it and lead it back to the necessity of the creation account, the day will fail me while I am presenting to you the great wisdom from the smallest things. “Let the earth sprout a fruit-bearing tree, producing fruit upon the earth” (Genesis 1:11). And immediately the mountain peaks were covered with foliage, and gardens were artfully arranged, and riverbanks were adorned with countless kinds of plants. Some had been prepared to adorn the human table; others were providing food for the herds, from their leaves and from their fruits. Others were furnishing us in advance with the benefits of medicine: their juices, their saps, their twigs, their barks, their fruit. And in a word, all the useful things that long experience has discovered for us, gathering what is beneficial from particular occurrences—these the keen forethought of the Creator, foreseeing them from the beginning, brought into being.

But you, whenever you see the cultivated plants, the wild ones, those that love water, those that grow on dry land, those that bear flowers, or those without flowers—recognizing the great in the small—always add to your wonder, and increase for me your love of the Creator. Examine how he made some plants evergreen, and others that are stripped bare; and among the evergreen ones, some shed their leaves, while others are ever-leafed. For both the olive and the pine shed their leaves, even if they exchange their foliage imperceptibly, so that they never seem to be stripped of their covering. But the date palm is ever-leafed, keeping the same leaf from its first sprouting to the end. Then consider also this: how the tamarisk is like an amphibious creature, numbered among the plants that love water, and yet multiplying in the deserts. For this reason Jeremiah fittingly compares the more wicked and wavering characters to this plant.
“Let the earth sprout” (Genesis 1:11). This small command was immediately a great nature and an artful principle, completing the countless properties of growing things more swiftly than our thought.

last_rejected.why: λεῖος means 'mild/gentle', not 'smooth'; describes taste, not texture.
last_rejected.ruling: λεῖος can mean 'smooth' to sense/taste; within normal range, not a meaning change.
πληκτικός = 'striking' is within normal range; not a meaning change or loss.
ἐκτραχύνω = 'roughens' is standard; 'hardens' is a preference, not an error.

last_rejected.why: ἐφιλοτεχνοῦντο is middle voice: 'paradises were fashioned with art/craft', not passive 'arranged'.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐφιλοτεχνοῦντο middle 'took pride in art' → 'artfully arranged' captures meaning adequately.

last_rejected.why: ηὐτρέπιστο is pluperfect middle: 'were preparing themselves/were made ready', but context suggests immediate creation, not prior preparation.
last_rejected.ruling: Pluperfect 'had been prepared' correctly renders ηὐτρέπιστο; prior preparation nuance is acceptable.

last_rejected.why: Imperfect tense: 'provided', not 'were providing' as ongoing; describes what they do.
last_rejected.ruling: Imfect 'were providing' is standard English imperfect rendering; not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: προεξένει is imperfect 'was furnishing/providing beforehand', singular; English plural 'were' mismatches singular subject.
last_rejected.ruling: προεξένει singular subject 'ἄλλα' (neuter plural) takes singular verb in Greek; English plural is normal.

last_rejected.why: λόγος here is 'word' or 'rational principle', not 'principle' alone; 'artful word' or 'skillful word' better captures Genesis creation by word.
last_rejected.ruling: λόγος ἔντεχνος as 'artful principle' captures rational/creative sense; 'word' is a preference.

last_rejected.quote: This small command was immediately a great nature
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὸ μικρὸν τοῦτο πρόσταγμα εὐθὺς φύσις μεγάλη καὶ λόγος ἔντεχνος ἦν
last_rejected.why: English omits 'was' (ἦν) placement, making 'immediately' modify 'was' unclear; but more seriously, 'nature' for φύσις misses that this command itself became/becomes a great nature.
last_rejected.fix: This small command was at once a great nature and a skillful word
last_rejected.ruling: English 'was immediately a great nature' includes ἦν; φύσις as 'nature' is correct, not omitted.
